opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I value most about that work, which became the ConvNeXt paper, is that it challenged a narrative that had become almost taken for granted at the time. Around 2020 and 2021, after vision transformers came out, there was a strong sense in the community that attention was the key ingredient and that convolutions were somehow outdated. People were attributing the gains of models like Swin Transformer to the self-attention mechanism itself.

What we tried to do was very simple in spirit. We started from a standard ResNet and gradually "modernized" it, step by step, borrowing design choices from transformers: the training recipe, the stage ratios, a patchify stem, depthwise convolutions, larger kernel sizes, an inverted bottleneck, replacing BatchNorm with LayerNorm, using GELU, fewer activation and normalization layers, and so on. At each step we measured what actually changed. And it turned out that a pure ConvNet, with no attention at all, could match or even outperform the hierarchical vision transformers on ImageNet, detection, and segmentation.

So the thing I value is less the specific architecture and more the methodology and the lesson. A lot of the improvement people credited to attention was really coming from many small design decisions and, very importantly, the training procedure. Just updating the training recipe alone gave a ResNet-50 a significant boost. That tells you that when we compare architectures, we often aren't comparing them fairly, because the surrounding details differ a lot.

I also like that the paper is, in a way, a kind of controlled scientific study rather than just proposing a new block. It encourages people to question which components really matter, and to be careful about attributing success to the most salient novelty. I think that mindset is useful well beyond vision architectures, for example when we think about what really drives progress in large language models or other foundation models today.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the study’s main value as challenging the belief that attention drove the gains and changing how people understand ConvNets versus vision transformers. It emphasizes the lesson about attribution and fair comparisons, rather than presenting component-by-component quantification as the main value.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that ConvNet locality gives an advantage when processing high-resolution images.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Ravid, it's great to be here. I think what I value most about that work, and I'm thinking of ConvNeXt in particular, is that it was really an exercise in intellectual honesty about where improvements actually come from.

When vision transformers arrived, there was this narrative that attention was the key ingredient, that ConvNets were fundamentally limited. And maybe that was true, but nobody had really checked. ViTs and Swin brought in a whole bundle of changes at once: different training recipes, longer schedules, different data augmentation, different normalization, larger kernels effectively through attention, different stage designs. The architecture got credit for all of it.

So the thing I'm proudest of is the methodology more than any single result. We started from a standard ResNet and modernized it one step at a time, controlling for everything else, and we wrote down what each change bought us. Training recipe alone closed a big chunk of the gap. Then things like the patchify stem, depthwise convolutions, inverted bottlenecks, larger kernels, swapping BatchNorm for LayerNorm, fewer activations. Each one is small and kind of boring on its own. Together they get you a pure ConvNet that matches or beats Swin at the same scale.

What I value about that is twofold. First, it gave the community a cleaner mental model: a lot of what looked like "attention is better" was really "modern training and macro design are better," and those are things you can port across architecture families. Second, it's a reminder that in deep learning, the controlled ablation is still one of the most useful tools we have. It's easy to publish a new block and a new number. It's harder, and I think more valuable, to say exactly which decisions matter and which are incidental.

And honestly, the result that the gap was largely about recipe rather than inductive bias changed how I think about architecture research in general. It made me more skeptical of big claims and more interested in the unglamorous details.

r001.rationale: The candidate emphasizes controlled ablations and documenting what each architectural change contributed, alongside changing the community’s understanding. It does not present that understanding as the study’s value rather than quantifying component contributions.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not suggest that ConvNet locality gives an advantage on high-resolution images.

astra-6.text:
What I value most is the understanding we gained from making a careful comparison. When we compare ConvNets and vision transformers, we’re often comparing more than two architectures—we’re also comparing different training recipes and design choices. So it’s hard to know where the improvement actually comes from.

By examining those details one at a time, we could ask which changes really matter and whether some of the advantages attributed to transformers could also benefit a ConvNet. For me, the exciting part isn’t just getting a better accuracy number. It’s questioning assumptions about why a model works and coming away with a clearer understanding of the design space.

sol-6.1.text:
What I value most is that it helped us question what was actually responsible for the progress we were seeing. When vision transformers started outperforming ConvNets, there were many differences beyond attention itself, including the training recipes and architectural choices. So we tried to disentangle those factors, gradually modernizing a conventional ConvNet and seeing how far it could go.

The result was that a pure ConvNet could be very competitive. To me, the important takeaway isn’t that convolution is better than attention. It’s that careful, controlled comparisons can change our understanding of where improvements come from. I find that kind of insight more valuable than just getting a higher number on a benchmark.
